result.summary: Achilles' ghost demands the sacrifice of Polyxena, who dies bravely, and Hecuba then finds her son Polydorus dead on the shore. She blinds the Thracian king Polymnestor and is turned into a barking dog. Aurora then begs Jove to honour her dead son Memnon, and his pyre's embers become the fighting Memnonides birds.

scenes.title: Achilles' ghost demands Polyxena
scenes.summary: Greek ships wait in Thrace when Achilles' shade rises and demands Polyxena's sacrifice at his tomb. The Greeks obey and lead her away.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk the ghost's anger if his honour is denied; Polyxena is to be killed.

scenes.title: Polyxena's brave sacrifice
scenes.summary: Polyxena bares her throat, asks to die free and to have her body returned to her mother. The priest strikes, and she dies modestly.
scenes.stakes: Polyxena faces death and the loss of her freedom and dignity.

scenes.title: Hecuba laments and finds Polydorus
scenes.summary: Hecuba mourns Polyxena, then goes to wash the body and sees Polydorus' corpse on the shore. Grief turns to rage and she plans revenge.
scenes.stakes: Hecuba has lost almost all her children and her freedom, and faces slavery.

scenes.title: Hecuba blinds Polymnestor
scenes.summary: Hecuba lures Polymnestor with a promised treasure, and with the captive women tears out his eyes. Attacked by Thracians, she turns into a barking dog.
scenes.stakes: Hecuba risks the vengeance of the Thracian people.

scenes.title: Aurora and the Memnonides
scenes.summary: Aurora pleads with Jove to honour her slain son Memnon. His pyre's embers become birds that fight each other yearly, and Aurora's tears become dew.
scenes.stakes: Aurora grieves for her dead son and wants him honoured.

alias_notes.explanation: The Odrysians were a Thracian people.
Hecuba's father in this tradition is Dymas.

notable_quotes.reason: Polyxena's dying care for modesty shows her nobility.
Hecuba's transformation into a barking dog.

analysis.text: The passage shows grief turning into vengeance and bodily transformation, with Hecuba's rage ending in an animal's bark.
Human sacrifice to a dead hero's ghost reflects ancient beliefs in honouring the dead and the fate of captive women after war.

legacy.text: Hecuba's story was dramatized by Euripides in Hecuba and later drawn on by Shakespeare, as in Hamlet's 'What's Hecuba to him?'

fun_facts.text: The Memnonides were said to return each year to fight at Memnon's tomb.

language_notes.text: Manes are the spirits of the dead, worshipped and appeased with offerings at the tomb.
The son of Atreus is Agamemnon, leader of the Greek expedition against Troy.
Refers to the Iliad quarrel, when Achilles nearly drew his sword on Agamemnon over the seizure of Briseis.
Pile means the funeral pyre; here it stands for Achilles' tomb.
Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, who carries out the sacrifice at his father's tomb.
Stygian means of the Styx, the river of the underworld; so, the realm of the dead.
Unconsumed means not burned; she asks that her body be returned for burial instead of being left or destroyed.
After Troy fell, Hecuba was assigned as a slave to Ulysses. The line says even he would have refused her, were she not Hector's mother.
Achilles killed Hector and other sons of Hecuba, and his ghost demanded Polyxena's sacrifice at his tomb.
Paris shot the arrow that killed Achilles, guided by Phœbus (Apollo). Hecuba hoped his death ended the threat.
'Descendant of Æacus' means Achilles, grandson of Æacus. Hecuba bitterly says she bore children only to feed his line's cruelty.
Pergamus was the citadel of Troy; she means only the fortress, or perhaps only her own suffering, still stands.
Penelope is Ulysses' wife. Hecuba imagines being given to her as a slave, a spectacle of fallen greatness.
'Foreign sand' means a hasty burial on the Thracian Chersonese shore, far from the Trojan royal tombs.
Polydorus, Hecuba's youngest son, was sent for safety to Polymestor, the Thracian king (Ismarian refers to Thrace).
Odrysian: Odrysae were a Thracian people; here it means Polymnestor, king of Thrace.
"Falsely swears" is ironic: Hecuba pretends to accept his oath and promise, while Polymnestor's own oath about her son was the lie.
The place was called Cynossema, 'dog's tomb', a landmark known to sailors; the note [55] refers to this name.
Pelasgian: here a poetic term for the Greeks. The 'wife and sister of Jove' is Juno.
Aurora favoured Troy because her son Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, fought as its ally against the Greeks.
The Memnonides were said to fight yearly at Memnon's tomb; the twelve signs of the Zodiac mean one year.
Daughter of Dymas is Hecuba; Dymas is named as her father in this tradition.

context_notes.text: Human sacrifice to a dead hero's ghost reflects the ancient belief that the unhonoured dead could demand offerings.
Priam was king of Troy and Hecuba's husband; Polyxena is their daughter, so Hecuba could once pay ransom with gold.
The Trojan women are captives awaiting distribution among the Greek victors, and gather around Polyxena, just sacrificed at Achilles' tomb.
Hecuba came to the shore to wash Polyxena's body. Polymestor had killed Polydorus for his gold, and the sea washed up the corpse.
Polymnestor, king of Thrace, had been trusted with Hecuba's son Polydorus and murdered him for his gold.
Aurora is the goddess of dawn, mother of Memnon, who was killed by Achilles.
Aurora's daily task is opening the day, bringing light as night ends.

literary_notes.text: Achilles' indignant questions shame the Greeks and show his pride in his own glory.
Polyxena offers her throat and breast herself, showing courage and dignity.
The crowd weeps while she holds back tears, contrasting victim and onlookers.
Her concern for modesty even as she falls makes her death deeply moving and ennobles her.
Hecuba addresses her dead daughter directly, making her lament intimate and intensifying the pathos.
Achilles' ashes 'rage' and act as an enemy, showing how even his death cannot end his harm.
Priam, once pitied for his fall, is now called happy, since he died before seeing worse sorrows.
Hecuba, struck silent by grief, is compared to hard rock, foreshadowing her later transformation into a dog.
Hecuba's grief turns to vengeful purpose, and she acts like a queen again, revealing her fierce, resolute nature.
Hecuba is compared to a lioness robbed of her cub, conveying animal ferocity before her transformation into a dog.
Hecuba's speech turning to barking completes the metamorphosis, fitting the animal imagery already used of her rage.
Dawn's colour fades and clouds hide the sky, so nature mirrors Aurora's grief.
The dark smoke from the pyre is likened to river mists that block the sun.
Dew is made of Aurora's tears, so a natural daily phenomenon becomes a memorial of maternal grief.
